     Falchions V. 26.1                                              2/26

1.​Implementation
The document has been created and approved by the General Assembly of 29.11.2025.
The document and its rules will be implemented from the 2029 season (01/01/2029).
Competitors will have 3 seasons to align their equipment with this document and its rules.



                     2.​Definition and Description
  2.1.​ Definition
“Falchion” is the term used to describe a single-edged bladed weapon from the Middle Ages in Europe.
The falchion originated in the 12th century and evolved until the 15th century.
Falchions can be one-handed or two-handed.
“Messer” is the term used to describe a specific subtype of falchion.


  2.2.​ Description
Falchions existed in many forms throughout the Middle Ages.
They have been classified by James Elmslie in 2015, and we will stick to his typology for buhurt.

Type of Falchions:

  ●​ Type 1
     A straight blade with a wider part on the striking edge.

  ●​ Type 2
     “Reverse-edged” forward curve, the point must be rounded or removed.

  ●​ Type 3
     Variations in having scalloped or cutaway tips on the blades.

  ●​ Type 4
     Curved saber-like blades often associated with, but not exclusive to, Eastern Europe.

  ●​ Type 5
     Symmetrical single-edged profiles with little to no curvature.

  ●​ 2-handed
     Not classified by James Elmslie , but depicted in manuscripts.


Falchions that are not based on the James Elmslie typology can be accepted if documented by historical
sources.




  Falchions V. 26.1                                                                                 3/26
Falchions V. 26.1   4/26

3.​General Requirements
Falchions of any types must:
  ●​   be based on historical sources,
  ●​   reproduce the proportions and curves based on historical sources,
  ●​   match the style of the armor kit of the competitor,
  ●​   be conform to the 9.0 section about pommels and guards,
  ●​   be conform to the Technical Requirements document for weapons.

All decorations on the falchion must be stylized in accordance with the style of the armor kit of the
competitor.

It is prohibited to decorate a falchion with images that are clearly modern and/or offensive. Any metal
part of the falchion must conform to the “Armors and Weapons Aesthetics and Decorations” document.

Any textile or leather part of the falchion must conform to the “Textiles and Leather” document.




  Falchions V. 26.1                                                                                 5/26

4.​Falchions Type 1
  4.1.​ Historical Sources and Datation
Type 1 falchions are based on Elmslie typology. They are characterized by a flaring profile, and broad,
abrupt tip.
There are 4 subtypes, from 1a to 1d.
All subtypes type 1 falchion have been used since the 13th century.
They are Approved for 14th century, Transitional and 15th century armors.
Type 1d falchion is Denied because its pointy edge is not safe.

5.​Falchions Type 2
  5.1.​ Historical Sources and Datation
Type 2 falchions are based on Elmslie typology. They are also called “reverse-edge falchions”. They are
sharpened along the ‘short’ edge, which features a clipped portion, leading to the reinforced thrusting tip.
They are Approved for 14th century, Transitional and 15th century armors.
A particular attention must be paid to the safety of the pointy edge, it must be made to be safe.

6.​Falchions Type 3
  6.1.​ Historical Sources and Datation
Type 3 falchions are based on Elmslie typology. They are characterized by having scalloped or cutaway
tips on the blades of various shapes. The curvature of the blade can vary.
There are 5 subtypes, from 3a to 3e.
All type 3 falchions have been used since the 14th century.
They are Approved for 14th century, Transitional and 15th century armors.
A particular attention must be paid to the safety of the pointy edge, it must be made to be safe.

7.​Falchions Type 4
  7.1.​ Historical Sources and Datation
Type 4 falchions are based on Elmslie typology. They are characterized by a curved blade that gives
them a sabre look.
There are 4 subtypes, from 4a to 4d.
All type 4 falchions have been used since the 14th century.
They are Approved for 14th century, Transitional and 15th century armors.

8.​Falchions Type 5
  8.1.​ Historical Sources and Datation
Type 5 falchions are based on Elmslie typology. They are characterized by relatively symmetrical
profiles, typically featuring little to no curvature over their length.
There are 5 subtypes, from 4a to 4e.
All type 5 falchions have been used since the 14th century.
Subtypes 5a, 5b, 5c falchions are Approved for 14th century, Transitional and 15th century armors.
Subtypes 5d and 5e are Denied for safety reasons.

9.​2-Handed Falchions
  9.1.​ Historical Sources and Datation
2-handed falchions are not based on Elmslie typology. They are depicted in manuscripts from the middle
ages in Europe.
There are 3 subtypes of 2-handed that are suitable for buhurt:
  ●​ Type 2
     It has a similar shape to 1-handed falchion type 2, with a square guard.
  ●​ Type 3c
     It has a similar shape to 1-handed falchion type 3c.
  ●​ Type 3e
     It has a similar shape to 1-handed falchion type 3e.


They are Approved for 14th century, Transitional and 15th century armors.

10.​Pommels and Guards
 10.1.​ Pommels
Pommels can be of many forms and designs, mainly of rounded or square shape.
Pommels shapes are sorted under the Oakeshott Typology.
Pommels can be decorated.
Any metal part of the pommel must conform to the “Armors and Weapons Aesthetics and Decorations”
document.


Example of historical shapes from OakeshottTypology:




Types A to E are all Denied as they are from centuries that predate the 14th century.


Types G1 and G2 originated from the 16th century.
They are:
  ●​ Approved for 16th century armors and weapons.
  ●​ Denied for 14th century, Transitional and 15th century armors and weapons.




  Falchions V. 26.1                                                                          21/26

10.2.​ Guards
Guards can be of many forms and designs, mainly of straight design for 14th and 15th century designs.
It is recommended to avoid exotic shapes of guards and stick to the classic shapes, widely supported by
historical sources.
Guards can be decorated.
Any metal part of the pommel must conform to the “Armors and Weapons Aesthetics and Decorations”
document.


Example of historical shapes from Oakeshott Typology:




                                  © Ewatt Oakeshott - The Sword in the Age of Chivalry



Note: Oakeshott defined up to 12 different styles of guards, with variations.
We selected only the first 6 styles to keep the document simple, but other styles of guards from the
Oakeshott typology are acceptable to use.



   Falchions V. 26.1                                                                                   23/26

11.​Common Mistakes
  11.1.​ 1-Handed Falchions with D-guards
From the 16th century, mainly in Italy, falchions with “D Guard” started to be used for civil combats.
They represent a serious risk of injury and can not be used.


All 1-handed falchions reproducing the designs of a 1-handed falchion with a D-guard are Denied.




    1.1.​ Examples of Denied Reproductions




                                          Picture from Medieval Extreme ©




   Falchions V. 26.1                                                                                     24/26

11.2.​ Beidanas
Beidanas are a farming tool from the 17th century in Italy. Despite its falchion inspired design, it is not a
weapon for combat and therefore not suitable for buhurt.


All falchions reproducing the designs of a Beidana are Denied.




  11.3.​ Falchions from the Morgan Bible (or Maciejowski Bible)


This manuscript is often used for falchions sources. But it originated from the middle of the 13th century,
and its design is unsafe for our sport.


All falchions reproducing the designs from this manuscript are Denied.




   Falchions V. 26.1                                                                                     25/26
